name: Lagrangian
tagline: Animation with real physics: springs that keep their momentum when interrupted, throws with friction onto snap points, and a small 2D world with gravity, collisions, joints and rolling. About 10 kB.
seoTitle: Lagrangian – physics-based animation: interruptible springs, inertia, gravity and collisions
description:
Most web animation is a curve over a fixed duration. Click twice and the element stops dead and starts again; throw it and it ignores how fast you threw. Lagrangian animates with physics instead. Its springs are the exact solution of the damped oscillator, so they know their position and velocity at every moment and simply continue when the target changes, at any frame rate.

Drag an element and Lagrangian measures how fast you let go, lets it glide with friction like iOS scrolling, rubber-bands past the edges and lands exactly on the nearest snap point. For playful interfaces there is a small 2D world: round and rectangular bodies with gravity, restitution and Coulomb friction, so they bounce, slide and roll, plus springs, hinges, rods and motors between bodies, sensors for drop zones and a pointer joint for grabbing and throwing. When the user asks for reduced motion, automatic motion jumps to its end.

faq.q: How is this different from Sigmoid?
faq.a: Sigmoid ties motion to the scroll position with native CSS scroll timelines and turns springs into CSS easing curves. Lagrangian runs physics in real time: interruptible springs, gestures, throws, gravity and collisions. They work well together.

Both are excellent and do far more, such as layout animations and timelines. Lagrangian focuses on the physics: exact springs, throws that land on snap points and a world with collisions and rolling, in about 10 kB.

faq.q: Is it a game physics engine?
faq.a: No. Bodies are circles and rotating boxes with hinges, rods and motors, which keeps the engine small. It is meant for playful interfaces. For arbitrary polygons and thousands of bodies use Matter.js or Rapier.
Springs and throws jump to where they would come to rest, so the layout ends up the same. Dragging and the world still follow the pointer, because the user is moving them.

Finished interface pieces built on the free physics: a bottom sheet, a side drawer, a dialog, a carousel, pull to refresh, a toast stack, a tab indicator, a page effect that lets a section fall apart, a drag-and-drop board for grids and columns, zoom and pan, a swipe stack, sortable lists, layout transitions, jelly deformation, ropes and impact sounds, with React hooks. The free library stays free and keeps everything it has today.

faq.q: Do my customers need a licence?
faq.a: No. You can use Lagrangian Pro in any number of websites and apps you build. Your customers only need a licence if they use it outside the project you delivered.
Yes. Items can be picked up with Space, moved with the arrow keys and dropped with Space or Enter, and every step is announced to screen readers. You can translate the announcements.
